detail: The road turns to slurry and the world narrows to ten feet in every direction.
A flat grey sky the colour of old iron presses down, muffling sound and draining colour from everything beneath it.
Shadows fall at angles that don't match the sun — pointing east when they should point west, stretching toward the light instead of away.
The DOL's golden light blankets the land without warmth, bright as a verdict and just as final.
The moon simply does not rise — the sky is stars only, and the dark between them feels deliberate.
Fine mineral dust from the Ars Lapis quarries has drifted far on the wind, coating the air with a dry, coppery taste.
The temperature drops without warning in the early afternoon, as if the season decided to skip ahead.
A reddish mist clings to low ground, smelling faintly of iron — travellers report it feels thicker the longer you stand still.
At dawn, a second sun-coloured light blooms on the western horizon for twenty minutes before fading — no one has explained it.
No wind at all — flames burn perfectly vertical, sounds carry absurdly far, and the stillness makes everyone uneasy.
Cold rain that isn't quite ice coats every surface in a thin glaze by nightfall.
A hot, acrid breeze blows in from the direction of the mines, carrying the faint smell of something burnt deep underground.
The sun sets but the sky never quite darkens, holding a dull, pewter half-light for hours past dusk.
Dozens of shooting stars cross the sky over the course of an hour — not randomly, but all moving in the same direction.
A hard overnight freeze leaves everything crystallised by morning — beautiful, treacherous, and strangely silent.
Cloud cover sits at head-height in the valleys, reducing visibility to near-zero and making the hills seem to float above nothing.
Perfect weather — the kind that makes experienced travellers in Le'Choix stop and wonder what's about to happen.
Snow falls horizontally, roads vanish, and distance becomes a suggestion.
The sun is half-covered by something — no official eclipse was announced by the DOL, and the silence from Ars Cultura is notable.
The full moon is so bright that shadows are sharp-edged and the night feels like an overexposed afternoon.
